newsitem.title: UK: Seasonal cheer passes nickel by as prices slump.
newsitem.headline: Seasonal cheer passes nickel by as prices slump.

text.p: As metal trading business winds down for Christmas and New Year celebrations in London, the nickel market outlook for 1997 is a little more bleak.
On Tuesday on the London Metal Exchange (LME) world nickel prices slipped to fresh 2-1/4 year lows, weighed down by speculative selling, long liquidation and rising LME stocks.
While traders and analysts were slow to read too much into the latest losses, ample metal supply could delay any significant recovery until well into 1997.
"This weakness is largely seasonal," said one major producer source. "The market is dead as many plants are closed, and we expect prices to remain around $6,500 (a tonne) for the rest of the year."
Benchmark three month nickel futures hit a low of $6,490 a tonne in early inter-office trade on Tuedsay, down $25 from the close on Monday and well away from the 1996 high hit in February of $8,850.
While demand tends to be slow over the new year period, a background of rising stocks has undermined prices since July.
"The clearest indication that demand for nickel is not strengthening is that LME stocks are still rising," said Robin Bhar, analyst at Brandeis (Brokers) Ltd.
"They are almost at 50,000 tonnes and at a level where we were a year or so ago," he added.
On Tuesday nickel stocks rose 150 tonnes to 49,548 tonnes, the highest level since November 1995.

Demand has failed to match expectations at the beginning of 1996, while big off-exchange stockpiles of Russian nickel in Europe and stainless steel scrap metal around the world have further dampened primary nickel consumption.
The fate of the market next year is largely in the hands of the stainless steel industry, which accounts for two thirds of Western world nickel offtake.
Analysts expect a pick-up in stainless steel production in 1997, but the impact on primary nickel demand will not be immediate.
"We are of the opinion that de-stocking still has some way to go," said Bhar. "It may not be until mid-1997 that nickel starts to recover."
"We are feeling fairly positive for the market in 1997. But there is still a reasonable amount of nickel around, so we won't get a reaction straight away," another analyst added.
A further cause for concern among dealers is the vulnerable technical outlook for the market, which may influence the way funds and speculative players trade.
"The immediate target remains $6,450, but we repeat that the longer term possibility is a fall into the $6,000/6,200 region," said David Charters of Investment Research of Cambridge.
"A head and shoulders pattern was confirmed about a month ago, which gave a reading of around $6,200," Bhar said.
